commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

content.text:
**The Keeper of Low Tide Light**

For thirty-one years, Walter Brannock climbed the spiral stairs of Gull Rock Light every evening at dusk, wound the clockwork that turned the great lens, and trimmed the wicks of the lamp. He did it so long that his knees learned the count of the steps before his mind did: one hundred and four, with a landing at sixty-two where the window looked westward over the water.

The sea glass started on the landing.

It was a small green thing, no bigger than a lentil, wedged in the mortar between two granite blocks. Walter had noticed it the way one notices a stray button or a bird feather, and he had flicked it away with his thumb. But the next evening it caught the last of the sun, and it seemed to glow with a light that had nothing to do with the lamp. He pried it free and held it up to his eye. The edges were worn soft and frosted, as though the sea had spent a long time sanding away every sharp thing about it.

He put it in his shirt pocket. That was the beginning.

Over the following years the pocket became a habit, and then a jar, and then a collection that filled three wooden crates in the storeroom beneath the lamp. Walter sorted it by color on the long winter nights when the fog came in so thick he could not see the rail from the gallery. Bottle-green from old wine and beer bottles. Cobalt from medicine vials, which were rare, and which he treated like coins. Amber from whisky and ale. The occasional milky white from ceramic, and once, astonishingly, a piece of ruby red that a supply captain swore came from a railway lantern lost in a wreck off the point before the war.

Most of it came from the cove on the eastern side of the island, where the tide pulled the rubbish of two centuries into a tangle of kelp and stone. Walter walked it every morning at low water, his head down, his eyes sweeping the wet sand the way a hound works a field. He found things the sea had been polishing for decades: a doll's blue shoe, a pipe bowl, a child's marble with a twist of white inside it. He kept the marble on the windowsill above his cot, where the lamp's passing beam lit it once every twelve seconds.

His wife, Ingrid, had called the collection foolish. She said so with affection, usually while she was hanging laundry on the line behind the keeper's cottage. "You have a lighthouse full of treasure and you spend your days looking at the ground," she would say. Then she would come down to the cove with him anyway, carrying a basket, and find a few pieces of her own. She found the best one, a rounded shard of cobalt the size of a plum stone, the summer before she died.

After the funeral, the cove felt different. The boat from the mainland came twice a week now instead of once, bringing supplies and the occasional inspector, and the young relief keeper, a sharp-faced man named Tobias Renn, had been sent out to learn the station. Tobias thought the sea glass was charming, in the way one thinks a hobby is charming. He did not understand the habit.

"Why do you keep it?" he asked one evening, as they sat with cold tea while the lens turned slowly above them, throwing its white arm across the water every twelve seconds.

Walter considered the question. He had been asked it by the mainland officials, by the boat crews, by Ingrid, and he had never answered it well.

"Because it was something that was broken," he said finally. "Something somebody threw away, or lost, or smashed on a rock. And the sea took all of that and worked on it for years, and it didn't make it sharp again. It made it gentle. Nobody planned that. It just happened, slowly, because something kept touching it."

Tobias said nothing. Outside, the light swept past.

"I suppose," Walter went on, "I like to think a man could be like that. Worn down by the right things. Not sharp anymore, but still holding light."

The next morning the fog lay thick on the cove and the tide was far out. Walter went down alone, as he always did, and worked the wet sand with his head bent low. He found a fragment of green near the waterline, then a second, then a larger piece of amber that had lost nearly all its edges. He held each one up to the gray sky and turned it over in his palm.

Tobias came down the rocks near noon, carrying two tin cups of coffee. He stopped at the bottom of the path and watched the old man on his knees in the sand.

"Find anything?" Tobias called.

Walter looked up. His face was lined and weathered, and there was a softness in it that the younger man had not seen before.

"Yes," Walter said. "Come and look. You have to hold it up to the light."

Tobias set the cups down on a flat stone and crossed the sand. Walter opened his palm. In the center lay a small piece of green glass, frosted and rounded, glowing faintly in the thin gray daylight.

Tobias knelt beside him, and for a long moment neither of them spoke. Then Walter closed his fingers gently over the glass and pressed it into the younger man's hand.

"Keep this one," he said. "You'll want something to remember the place by."

---
